step.title: Frame a selection, keep its coordinates
step.goal: Make Fit frame the selected object, without changing its geometry or hiding distant objects through the far plane.
step.trace: Fit → Editor chooses selected or all bounds → Camera targets those bounds → scene extent keeps depth coverage
step.question: Why do the fitted radius and the scene extent need separate values?
step.answer: The selected object’s radius decides how closely to frame it and how far zoom may travel. The extent of the whole scene decides how far depth and pick rays must reach. Using the small selected radius for both could clip an unrelated distant object.
step.story:
Imagine selecting one beam in a building. You want to look closely at that beam, not shrink every coordinate in the building. Fit changes the camera. It must leave the stored model untouched.

The production viewer already follows this rule: Fit frames the selection, or everything when nothing is selected. Our course has one selected object so far. Later, multiple selection will combine the bounds of all selected objects.

![The selected bounds choose the camera target and distance; the whole scene supplies depth coverage.](../illustrations/journey-26.svg)

**Keep the owners clear.** Scene measures vertices. Editor chooses which objects matter for this request. Camera decides where to look. Renderer needs no new branch: it receives the next matrix as before.

There is one trap. Fitting a small beam makes the camera radius small. If the far plane also shrinks to that radius, another visible object farther behind it can disappear. We separate radius, which controls framing and zoom, from extent, which covers the whole scene.

The coordinates remain model values. A triangle whose sides are 1, 1000 or 0.001 units can occupy the same screen space after Fit. That does not tell us whether its file means metres or millimetres; the following units lesson makes that convention explicit.
step.result:
Type `Example Box`, `View Isometric`, `View Orthographic`, then `Fit`. Now type `Select Next` three times to select the box. Submit `Fit` again: the yellow box becomes the focus. Repeat Fit; the picture should stay still.

Type `Undo`: adding the box is undone, while the camera stays where Fit placed it. `Redo` restores the box. Click empty space to clear selection, then run `Fit` to see the whole scene again. Try the same sequence in perspective.
step.experiment: Before running the scale test, predict whether multiplying every vertex by 1000 should make its fitted picture 1000 times wider. It should not: Fit also moves the camera farther away. Then temporarily replace extent with radius in the far-plane calculation. Run the distant-picking test, explain the failure, and restore extent.
step.production: Fit now follows the production selection-or-all rule. The production viewer combines multiple selected rows and has tighter corner-based fitting, model-unit conversion and reversed depth. Those remain visible tasks in the course plan; this lesson introduces the shared responsibility boundary without claiming those parts are complete.
step.browser_status: Fit frames the selection, or the whole scene when nothing is selected.
step.browser_caption: Actual Chrome checkpoint after typed commands frame the selected box. Its yellow highlight, closer camera and unchanged companion geometry distinguish this lesson from fitting the whole scene.

edits.why: Use one bounds loop for all objects or one stable ID. None means no selection filter; is_some_and skips a row only when an ID was supplied and differs.
